title: Prompting Claude to falsify your default retrieval assumptions
text: Four, where you cut decides what can be found and there's no universally correct size. Chapter five, approximate search trades recall for speed and the trade is a number you set. Chapter six, sparse and dense fail on different queries and combining them usually helps, but this run was one of the times it did not. Three layers, three tradeoffs, and not one of them ships with a default you can install and forget. Your turn. Paste this. Here are the three retrieval decisions I've made by default: my chunk size, my index's accuracy setting, and my choice of retriever. For each one, tell me what measurement would prove it wrong on my data, and what the cheapest version of that measurement looks like. The second half is the part that earns its keep. Anything will hand you best practices. Asking what would falsify each choice, and what the cheap version of that test costs, is what turns three inherited defaults into three decisions you can actually defend. There is no default, Vedanshi Dakshesh Patel.
